newsitem.title: UK: Britons complain about cross-border European ads.
newsitem.headline: Britons complain about cross-border European ads.

text.p: Consumers in Britain are complaining more about cross-border advertising than people in other European countries, while, ironically, ads created in Britain are coming under the most fire across Europe, according to figures released on Wednesday.

The European Advertising Standards Alliance (EASA) said in its July newsletter that 29 percent of all cross-border complaints about advertising in Europe in 1996 were made by consumers in Britain and 19 percent by people in Ireland.

Cross-border complaints are described as those in which a consumer makes a written complaint to a regulatory or self-regulatory body in his or her country about advertising that originated in another country.
The EASA said 16 percent of complaints last year came from consumers in France and 13 percent each from Germany and Luxembourg.
Oliver Gray, director general of the EASA, said Britons might be making a relatively large number of complaints because they were more "complaint literate" than consumers in some other countries.

He also told Reuters ads created in Britain might be prompting more complaints than those from other countries because English-language ads were more accessible to consumers in Ireland and other countries than some non-English-language advertising.

Most complaints in 1996 were about advertising considered misleading by consumers, while the number of complaints about ads considered offensive has dropped significantly since 1995. "It might be that advertisers ... are becoming more aware of what might offend people," Gray said. "We've recommended that people be much more cautious on these issues," he said, referring to subjects like advertising aimed at children and ads that uses sexual themes.
The EASA said consumers complained the most about ads carried in the press or by direct mail or fax, while there were few complaints about television commercials.
It said Britain was the country where the largest number of questionable ads were created in 1996, representing 15 of the total 47 complaints filed.
The Netherlands came next with seven complaints, France represented six and Belgium originated five.
The advertising industry in Europe is trying to show national governments and the European Commission it is capable of protecting consumers by regulating itself.
A main goal of the industry is to avoid statutory regulation of the advertising and marketing sectors.

Countries in Western Europe, like Britain, the Netherlands and Belgium, have self-regulatory bodies that oversee the advertising sector, while Germany and France, which have the biggest advertising markets in Europe, have tighter regulation.

The cross-border issue is a tricky subject because some consumers object to some advertising or direct mail they get from other countries, but industry executives say advertising should be protected by European Union rules of free trade.
They say advertising that is legal in one European Union country should be allowed in others, just like any other goods or services.
One senior advertising executive said recently an elderly man in Britain and his wife were upset when he received unsolicited pornographic literature by post from a company in the Netherlands.

But when Britain's Advertising Standards Authority complained to its counterpart organisation in Amsterdam -- and said it was illegal in Britain to send pornography by post -- the latter said that kind of unsolicited direct mail was legal and acceptable in the Netherlands, and it would take no action.
